questions.csvField:
3) Case Question: Duolingo, a language-learning platform that leverages gamification and streak mechanics to make education engaging, is looking to deepen brand affinity and daily usage among college students. The company is seeking innovative and impactful strategies that fit naturally into student routines and campus culture. Previous growth has come from marketing Duolingo’s bite-sized daily lessons, social leaderboard competition, and viral, unhinged social media presence. 
Your task is to develop a comprehensive marketing campaign for Duolingo focusing on increasing brand awareness and daily app engagement among college students. (Max 300 words)

questions.label: Supreme Case — all four questions graded per UMA's answer key

anchors.description: No structure at all, just a guessed number; ignores the channel breakdown; confuses total apparel market size with the premium/hype niche.
Attempts a structure but shakily — doesn't segment by channel, or lands on an implausible number without sanity-checking it.
Clear top-down/bottom-up structure stated aloud, segments by the four channels as prompted, lands on a sanity-checked, defensible range (roughly $1-5B).
Solid structure plus partial bonus — a real anchor data point or explicit channel ranking by price sensitivity — but doesn't fully separate Supreme's addressable slice from the whole category.

Distinguishes total spend from Supreme's addressable/incremental slice, flags resale as a transfer market unprompted, uses a real anchor data point, and explicitly ranks channels by price sensitivity with a stated reason.

criteria.name: Q2. Gen Z Trends & Campaign Tie

anchors.description: Generic ideas with no real mechanism or tie to Supreme's scarcity/growth tension — e.g. "do a TikTok campaign."
Names some Gen Z trends but the campaign tie is vague or generic (e.g. just "campus ambassador program" with no specifics).

Covers most core trends (status via scarcity/access, community/subculture affiliation, authenticity, resale/investment mindset, campus social currency) and ties them to a solid campaign idea like a campus-exclusive drop.
Solid trend coverage plus a named, reasonably specific mechanism — approaching bonus territory.

A named, specific mechanism (a real campus takeover tour, a verified-purchase community app, a student-designer contest that actually ships) plus meaningful engagement with the Gen Z data referenced in the prompt.
Doesn't identify either side clearly, or ignores the scarcity/dilution tension entirely.
Names some challenges or opportunities but generically, without connecting them to Supreme's specific situation (the two acquisitions, drop fatigue already in the prompt).
Covers real challenges (dilution, drop fatigue, counterfeits, acquisition instability) and real opportunities (a fresh cohort with no fatigue, campus's inherent scarcity, resale-driven loyalty).
Solid coverage plus a concrete proposal for how to expand without diluting scarcity.

A concrete anti-dilution mechanism (geographic/quantity caps baked into the program itself), ties the acquisition instability point to a specific recommendation, and treats counterfeit risk as a creative opportunity (authentication tech) as well as a threat.
Lists several disconnected ideas with no prioritization or clear #1 recommendation.
States a recommendation, but it doesn't clearly reference the scarcity/growth tension or thread the earlier analysis together.
Converges on one (at most two) primary recommendation, explicitly threads the scarcity/growth tension, and briefly references the market size and Gen Z insight from earlier answers.
Solid convergence plus a distinctive name or framing for the idea.
A memorable, nameable big idea (a real program/campaign name) plus an explicit proposed success metric — resale price stability, repeat purchase rate, waitlist/demand ratio.
Passive in discussion; ideas mostly come from others.

Strong collaboration & contribution, just short of the top mark.

questions.label: HeyTea Case — all three questions graded per UMA's answer key

anchors.description: No real math shown, or a conversion rate with no reasoning behind it.
Picks a conversion rate and does the arithmetic, but doesn't sanity-check whether the campaign actually pays for itself, or draws the wrong conclusion from their own numbers.

Picks a plausible conversion rate (well under 1% is realistic), shows the arithmetic through to a revenue number, and correctly recognizes that direct-response payback rarely works cleanly for an awareness campaign at that price point.
Solid math plus a partial move toward LTV reasoning — mentions repeat visits matter but doesn't fully build the case.

Reaches the "aha": brings in repeat-visit/LTV as the real payback lens, explicitly separates brand/awareness value from direct conversion value, and sensitivity-checks their own assumption ("if conversion were 2x higher/lower...").
Suggests only one-off ideas, or leans on discounting despite the brand's premium positioning.
Names a loyalty or community idea but it's generic, or accidentally still discount-flavored.
Proposes non-discount retention mechanics — stamp cards/exclusive unlocks, seasonal limited drops, community events, membership perks — that fit HeyTea's premium positioning.
Solid retention ideas plus a stated retention metric to track, without fully avoiding discount-flavored framing.
Explicitly avoids discount-flavored language even in loyalty mechanics, proposes a concrete retention metric (e.g. 30-day repeat visit rate), and names a real comparable brand mechanic as an analogy.
Doesn't engage with the delivery-preference tension at all.
Names an in-store-exclusive idea but doesn't explain why it would actually pull someone away from delivery.
Proposes in-store-exclusive items, Instagrammable experiences, or loyalty perks tied to physical visits, and notes the sensory/experiential parts of the drink that degrade in delivery.
Solid tactics plus recognition that HeyTea may not want to fully fight delivery — some segmentation between in-store hype and everyday delivery demand.
Recognizes the segmentation tension explicitly, and reuses the Gen Z status/community insight from the Supreme case (an in-store visit as social content) — real pattern transfer across cases.

criteria.name: Trend Awareness ("marketing strategy that captured your attention")

anchors.description: Picks something outdated or vague ("Nike's marketing is good"), or can't explain why it worked beyond "I saw it a lot."
Names something specific and recent but the explanation of why it worked is thin.
Names something specific and recent, and explains the actual mechanism of why it worked.
Solid answer plus a partial connection to a broader trend.
Connects it to a broader trend (attention economy, community-driven marketing, nostalgia) and generalizes a lesson from it — the same analytical instinct the case questions are testing.

criteria.name: Motivation & Fit ("what motivates you beyond your professional goals")

anchors.description: Purely resume-driven — "looks good on my resume" — with no personal connection to UMA.
Somewhat genuine but generic — could be said about any club.
Genuine, specific answer beyond resume-building — real community, specific people or culture at UMA, specific project types.
Solid answer that's clearly genuine, just short of a concrete callback.
Ties back to something concrete from the social round the day before — real evidence of engagement, not a canned answer.
No real example, or one where they didn't actually persuade anyone — the example doesn't match the question asked.
A real attempt to persuade someone, but the story reveals little about what specifically they did or why it worked.
A genuine example with a clear, specific tactic they used to shift someone's view — competent but unremarkable.
A genuine example plus real insight into why the tactic worked, pointing at a transferable persuasion skill rather than a one-off.
A unique, substantive experience where the specific approach and the lesson they took from it show real, transferable judgment about persuading people — not a rehearsed talking point.
No real example, or one where they didn't actually identify or act on anything themselves — the example doesn't match the question asked.
A real attempt at improving something, but the story reveals little about what they actually noticed or changed.
A genuine example where they clearly identify a gap and describe concrete steps they personally took — competent but unremarkable.
A genuine example plus real insight into why the change mattered, pointing at a transferable instinct for spotting and fixing problems.
A unique, substantive experience showing genuine initiative and a transferable lesson about improving a process or system — not a rehearsed talking point.
Rambling, a generic resume readout with no tailoring to UMA specifically.
Reasonably clear but not obviously tailored to why they want UMA.
Clear and concise, at least somewhat tailored to why they want UMA rather than a generic resume readout.
Clear, concise, and well-tailored across most of the interview.
Clear, concise, and well-tailored to UMA across the entire interview, including a sharp "tell me about yourself" that isn't just a resume readout.

questions.csvField:
3) Case Question: This company (name ideas may include but are not limited to: WeatherDrop, SkySupply, Cloudly) is an on-demand weather delivery service that lets customers customize and schedule the perfect weather for any occasion. From sunshine and snow to thunderstorms and fog, users can order atmospheric conditions straight to their location. 
1) Create a poster or website landing page for a fictional weather delivery company. 
2) Create a simple logo and include this logo on your website or poster. 
Consider font, color, and imagery in your deliverable and create a compelling narrative that clearly sells the product to target audiences. 
(We recommend using Figma for website designs and Adobe products such as Illustrator or Photoshop for posters, but feel free to use whichever medium you feel most comfortable with.) 
3) Please share a link to your design along with a document explaining your design process and decisions as a Google Drive link. Make sure to share it with us! (Max 300 words)
